slides.question: According to Shapin, what do both industrial and academic scientists most want?

options.explanation: While money is discussed, it's not described as the primary want.

options.text: Environments where they can do interesting work with some degree of freedom
options.explanation: Shapin says: 'both industrial and academic scientists seem to want environments in which they can do interesting work and, perhaps, to enjoy a degree of freedom.'
Not identified as the primary shared goal.

options.text: Strict separation between pure and applied research
options.explanation: Shapin argues this contrast is overstated.

lessons.title: Key Terms
lessons.description: Vocabulary from An Interview with Steven Shapin.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Giving someone a sense of dignity and honour
slides.context: Used to describe how science was historically seen as morally elevating.
slides.example: Science was historically seen as ennobling — those who studied nature were made virtuous through that study.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Favourable or likely to lead to success
slides.context: Used to describe conditions favorable for scientific inquiry.
slides.example: Some sorts of modern industry can offer more propitious conditions for scientific inquiry than some sorts of universities.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Selfless concern for the well-being of others
slides.context: Present among scientists working in industry who hope their work benefits humanity.
slides.example: One ought not neglect aspects of altruism, even utopianism, that one can find among scientists working in industry.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: Insisting that one's opinions are correct without considering other views
slides.context: Used to describe a presumption about pure vs. applied research quality.
slides.example: A presumption that applied research requires less brain-power than pure research is just dogmatic.
